cityPlaces.name: Statio of the First Cohort of Vigiles
cityPlaces.summary: Barracks of the cohort covering Regions VII (Via Lata) and IX (Circus Flaminius). Remains seen in the 17th century between San Marcello al Corso and Santi Apostoli included large halls and statues, among them a Genius of the cohort, and many dedications to emperors by the cohort come from the same spot.
scholarship: Sablayrolles, Libertinus miles: les cohortes de vigiles (1996)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Cohortium Vigilum Stationes
Platner and Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929) s.v. Cohortium Vigilum Stationes
Lanciani, Forma Urbis Romae (1893-1901) pl. 22
cityPlaces.note: End date conjectural: the vigiles are last securely attested in the 4th century; fire-fighting passed to the urban prefecture and the collegia. Position from the 1644 discoveries reported by Lanciani; the barracks probably filled a whole block west of Piazza Santi Apostoli.

cityPlaces.name: Statio of the Second Cohort of Vigiles
cityPlaces.summary: Station of the cohort for Regions III and V, on the Esquiline plateau near the later church of Santa Bibiana, inside the Aurelian circuit and just behind the line of the Servian agger. Vigiles inscriptions found here and Pirro Ligorio's note of a large building destroyed in the 16th century fix the area.
scholarship: Sablayrolles, Libertinus miles: les cohortes de vigiles (1996)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Cohortium Vigilum Stationes
Platner and Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929) s.v. Cohortium Vigilum Stationes
cityPlaces.note: End date conjectural: the vigiles are last securely attested in the 4th century; fire-fighting passed to the urban prefecture and the collegia. Exact footprint unknown; placed on Via Giolitti by Santa Bibiana.

cityPlaces.name: Statio of the Third Cohort of Vigiles
cityPlaces.summary: Station of the cohort for Regions IV and VI, listed by the Regionary Catalogues in Region VI (Alta Semita). Vigiles inscriptions south of the Baths of Diocletian suggest it stood on the Viminal ridge between the baths and the Vicus Patricius.
scholarship: Sablayrolles, Libertinus miles: les cohortes de vigiles (1996)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Cohortium Vigilum Stationes
Platner and Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929) s.v. Cohortium Vigilum Stationes
cityPlaces.note: End date conjectural: the vigiles are last securely attested in the 4th century; fire-fighting passed to the urban prefecture and the collegia. Only the general area is known.

cityPlaces.name: Statio of the Fourth Cohort of Vigiles
cityPlaces.summary: Station of the cohort for Regions XII and XIII, on the Piccolo Aventino by the church of San Saba. Inscriptions naming the cohort, including dedications by its officers, were found around San Saba and fix the barracks there, controlling the Aventine and the Emporium below.
scholarship: Sablayrolles, Libertinus miles: les cohortes de vigiles (1996)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Cohortium Vigilum Stationes
Platner and Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929) s.v. Cohortium Vigilum Stationes
cityPlaces.note: End date conjectural: the vigiles are last securely attested in the 4th century; fire-fighting passed to the urban prefecture and the collegia.

cityPlaces.name: Statio of the Fifth Cohort of Vigiles
cityPlaces.summary: Station of the cohort for Regions I and II, on the Caelian beside and below Santa Maria in Domnica (the Navicella). Two large marble rosters of the cohort dated AD 205 and 210 (CIL VI 1057-1058) and altars to the Genius of its centuries were found here in the 19th century, with a courtyard and portico.
scholarship: Sablayrolles, Libertinus miles: les cohortes de vigiles (1996)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Cohortium Vigilum Stationes
Platner and Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929) s.v. Cohortium Vigilum Stationes
cityPlaces.note: End date conjectural: the vigiles are last securely attested in the 4th century; fire-fighting passed to the urban prefecture and the collegia. The rosters list over 1,000 men, showing the cohort's strength after Septimius Severus.

cityPlaces.name: Statio of the Sixth Cohort of Vigiles
cityPlaces.summary: Station of the cohort for Regions VIII and X, placed by the Regionary Catalogues in Region VIII near the imperial fora. Its site has not been found; it probably lay on the slope between the Forum of Caesar and the Capitol along the Clivus Argentarius.
scholarship: Sablayrolles, Libertinus miles: les cohortes de vigiles (1996)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Cohortium Vigilum Stationes
Platner and Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929) s.v. Cohortium Vigilum Stationes
cityPlaces.note: End date conjectural: the vigiles are last securely attested in the 4th century; fire-fighting passed to the urban prefecture and the collegia. Location is a guess within Region VIII.

cityPlaces.name: Statio of the Seventh Cohort of Vigiles
cityPlaces.summary: Main barracks of the cohort for Regions XI and XIV (Transtiberim). Unlike its excavated guardhouse by San Crisogono, the station itself is unlocated; it probably stood in the dense lowland of Trastevere between Santa Maria in Trastevere and the river crossing at the Pons Aemilius.
scholarship: Sablayrolles, Libertinus miles: les cohortes de vigiles (1996)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Cohortium Vigilum Stationes
Platner and Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929) s.v. Cohortium Vigilum Stationes
cityPlaces.note: End date conjectural: the vigiles are last securely attested in the 4th century; fire-fighting passed to the urban prefecture and the collegia.

cityPlaces.name: Excubitorium of the Seventh Cohort (Trastevere)
cityPlaces.summary: Guardhouse of the seventh cohort excavated in 1866-1867 about 20 m south of San Crisogono, at the corner of Via di Monte Fiore and Via della VII Coorte. A Hadrianic house with a hexagonal basin in its court and a shrine (lararium) was converted into a post; more than 100 graffiti of the vigiles, dated AD 215-245 and invoking the 'Genius excubitori', cover its walls. The upper part stands about 8 m above the ancient floor.
scholarship: Sablayrolles, Libertinus miles: les cohortes de vigiles (1996)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Cohortium Vigilum Stationes
Platner and Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929) s.v. Cohortium Vigilum Stationes
Mols, 'L'excubitorium della VII coorte a Trastevere', Mededelingen Rome (2002)
cityPlaces.note: Reburied in 1966. Built as a house under Hadrian (brick stamps), used by the vigiles in the early 3rd century; the aedicula paintings are Severan.

cityPlaces.name: Excubitorium of Region I (Porta Capena)
cityPlaces.summary: One of the 14 guard posts listed by the 4th-century Regionary Catalogues ('cohortes VII vigilum habentes excubitoria XIIII'). Region I had no main station; its post, manned from the cohort V, probably stood beside the Via Appia south of the Porta Capena, between the Baths of Caracalla and the Caelian.
scholarship: Sablayrolles, Libertinus miles: les cohortes de vigiles (1996)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Cohortium Vigilum Stationes
Platner and Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929) s.v. Cohortium Vigilum Stationes
cityPlaces.note: Follows the view that the 14 excubitoria include the 7 stations, leaving one post in each of the 7 regions without a station. Position is a reasoned guess on a main street of the region. End date conjectural: the vigiles are last securely attested in the 4th century; fire-fighting passed to the urban prefecture and the collegia.

cityPlaces.name: Excubitorium of Region III (Isis et Serapis)
cityPlaces.summary: One of the 14 guard posts listed by the 4th-century Regionary Catalogues ('cohortes VII vigilum habentes excubitoria XIIII'). Region III had no main station; its post, manned from the cohort I, probably stood in the Oppian valley along the Via Labicana near the Ludus Magnus.
scholarship: Sablayrolles, Libertinus miles: les cohortes de vigiles (1996)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Cohortium Vigilum Stationes
Platner and Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929) s.v. Cohortium Vigilum Stationes
cityPlaces.note: Follows the view that the 14 excubitoria include the 7 stations, leaving one post in each of the 7 regions without a station. Position is a reasoned guess on a main street of the region. End date conjectural: the vigiles are last securely attested in the 4th century; fire-fighting passed to the urban prefecture and the collegia.

cityPlaces.name: Excubitorium of Region IV (Templum Pacis)
cityPlaces.summary: One of the 14 guard posts listed by the 4th-century Regionary Catalogues ('cohortes VII vigilum habentes excubitoria XIIII'). Region IV had no main station; its post, manned from the cohort III, probably stood in the Subura near the Vicus Patricius and the Clivus Suburanus.
scholarship: Sablayrolles, Libertinus miles: les cohortes de vigiles (1996)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Cohortium Vigilum Stationes
Platner and Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929) s.v. Cohortium Vigilum Stationes
cityPlaces.note: Follows the view that the 14 excubitoria include the 7 stations, leaving one post in each of the 7 regions without a station. Position is a reasoned guess on a main street of the region. End date conjectural: the vigiles are last securely attested in the 4th century; fire-fighting passed to the urban prefecture and the collegia.

cityPlaces.name: Excubitorium of Region IX (Circus Flaminius)
cityPlaces.summary: One of the 14 guard posts listed by the 4th-century Regionary Catalogues ('cohortes VII vigilum habentes excubitoria XIIII'). Region IX had no main station; its post, manned from the cohort I, probably stood in the central Campus Martius between the Theatre of Pompey and the Pantheon.
scholarship: Sablayrolles, Libertinus miles: les cohortes de vigiles (1996)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Cohortium Vigilum Stationes
Platner and Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929) s.v. Cohortium Vigilum Stationes
cityPlaces.note: Follows the view that the 14 excubitoria include the 7 stations, leaving one post in each of the 7 regions without a station. Position is a reasoned guess on a main street of the region. End date conjectural: the vigiles are last securely attested in the 4th century; fire-fighting passed to the urban prefecture and the collegia.

cityPlaces.name: Excubitorium of Region X (Palatium)
cityPlaces.summary: One of the 14 guard posts listed by the 4th-century Regionary Catalogues ('cohortes VII vigilum habentes excubitoria XIIII'). Region X had no main station; its post, manned from the cohort VI, probably stood on the Clivus Victoriae at the north-west corner of the Palatine.
scholarship: Sablayrolles, Libertinus miles: les cohortes de vigiles (1996)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Cohortium Vigilum Stationes
Platner and Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929) s.v. Cohortium Vigilum Stationes
cityPlaces.note: Follows the view that the 14 excubitoria include the 7 stations, leaving one post in each of the 7 regions without a station. Position is a reasoned guess on a main street of the region. End date conjectural: the vigiles are last securely attested in the 4th century; fire-fighting passed to the urban prefecture and the collegia.

cityPlaces.name: Excubitorium of Region XI (Circus Maximus)
cityPlaces.summary: One of the 14 guard posts listed by the 4th-century Regionary Catalogues ('cohortes VII vigilum habentes excubitoria XIIII'). Region XI had no main station; its post, manned from the cohort VII, probably stood in the Forum Boarium and Velabrum by the starting gates of the Circus Maximus.
scholarship: Sablayrolles, Libertinus miles: les cohortes de vigiles (1996)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Cohortium Vigilum Stationes
Platner and Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929) s.v. Cohortium Vigilum Stationes
cityPlaces.note: Follows the view that the 14 excubitoria include the 7 stations, leaving one post in each of the 7 regions without a station. Position is a reasoned guess on a main street of the region. End date conjectural: the vigiles are last securely attested in the 4th century; fire-fighting passed to the urban prefecture and the collegia.

cityPlaces.name: Excubitorium of Region XIII (Aventinus)
cityPlaces.summary: One of the 14 guard posts listed by the 4th-century Regionary Catalogues ('cohortes VII vigilum habentes excubitoria XIIII'). Region XIII had no main station; its post, manned from the cohort IV, probably stood on the river slope of the Aventine above the Emporium.
scholarship: Sablayrolles, Libertinus miles: les cohortes de vigiles (1996)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Cohortium Vigilum Stationes
Platner and Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929) s.v. Cohortium Vigilum Stationes
cityPlaces.note: Follows the view that the 14 excubitoria include the 7 stations, leaving one post in each of the 7 regions without a station. Position is a reasoned guess on a main street of the region. End date conjectural: the vigiles are last securely attested in the 4th century; fire-fighting passed to the urban prefecture and the collegia.

cityPlaces.name: Headquarters of the Praefectus Vigilum
cityPlaces.summary: Office of the equestrian prefect commanding the 3,500 to 7,000 vigiles, with judicial powers over arson, burglary and theft. Its site is unknown; scholars have suggested the area of the Crypta Balbi or the station of the first cohort by Santi Apostoli.
scholarship: Sablayrolles, Libertinus miles: les cohortes de vigiles (1996)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Cohortium Vigilum Stationes
Platner and Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929) s.v. Cohortium Vigilum Stationes
cityPlaces.note: Placed at the Crypta Balbi hypothesis; the alternative is the First Cohort's station.

cityPlaces.name: Castra Praetoria (seat of the Praetorian Guard)
cityPlaces.summary: Sejanus concentrated the nine (later more) praetorian cohorts, until then billeted around Rome and Italy, in a single camp on the Viminal plateau in AD 23; the urban cohorts shared it. It became the arena of imperial politics: Claudius was proclaimed here in 41, the empire auctioned here in 193. Constantine abolished the guard after the Milvian Bridge in 312 and demolished the inner wall.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Castra Praetoria
Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed. 2010)
Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000) s.v. Castra Praetoria
cityPlaces.note: The physical camp is in the buildings collection (castra_praetoria_mon); this record carries the institution.

cityPlaces.name: Castra Urbana (camp of the urban cohorts)
cityPlaces.summary: The urban cohorts, the city police under the praefectus urbi, lived in the Castra Praetoria until Aurelian gave them their own camp 'in campo Agrippae' in the 270s. It lay in Region VII east of the Via Lata, near the Forum Suarium whose pork distribution the cohorts supervised.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Castra Urbana
Coarelli, Rome and Environs: An Archaeological Guide (2007)
Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000) s.v. Castra Urbana
cityPlaces.note: Exact site unknown; placed in the Campus Agrippae between Via del Corso and Via del Tritone.

cityPlaces.name: Castra Peregrina
cityPlaces.summary: Camp on the Caelian of the frumentarii and other soldiers seconded from the provincial armies, who acted as couriers, supply officers and secret police. Remains, dedications to the Genius castrorum peregrinorum and a mithraeum were found under and north of Santo Stefano Rotondo.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Castra Peregrina
Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed. 2010)
Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000) s.v. Castra Peregrina

cityPlaces.name: Castra Priora Equitum Singularium
cityPlaces.summary: First barracks of the emperor's horse guard, the equites singulares Augusti, founded under Trajan. Remains with many altars of the guardsmen came to light in 1885-1886 on Via Tasso, north of the Lateran.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Castra Equitum Singularium
Speidel, Riding for Caesar (1994)
Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000)
cityPlaces.note: Disbanded by Constantine in 312 for supporting Maxentius.

cityPlaces.name: Castra Nova Equitum Singularium
cityPlaces.summary: Second barracks of the imperial horse guard, built under Septimius Severus when he doubled the unit. Constantine razed it after 312 and built the Lateran basilica on top; its walls and painted rooms survive beneath the nave of San Giovanni in Laterano.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed. 2010)
Speidel, Riding for Caesar (1994)

cityPlaces.name: Castra Misenatium
cityPlaces.summary: Quarters of the detachment of sailors from the fleet at Misenum, who worked the great awnings (velaria) of the Colosseum and staged naval shows. The Regionary Catalogues place it in Region III, near the amphitheatre along the Via Labicana.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Castra Misenatium
Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000)
cityPlaces.note: Exact site uncertain; placed east of the Ludus Magnus.

cityPlaces.name: Castra Ravennatium
cityPlaces.summary: Quarters in Trastevere of the sailors of the Ravenna fleet, probably connected with the naumachiae on the right bank. Listed in Region XIV by the Regionary Catalogues; often placed near San Callisto.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Castra Ravennatium
Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000)
cityPlaces.note: Location within Trastevere conjectural.

cityPlaces.name: Castra Lecticariorum
cityPlaces.summary: Barracks of the litter-bearers' guild in Region XIV, listed in the Regionary Catalogues. The litter carriers of the wealthy were organised as a corporation and lodged together in Trastevere.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Castra Lecticariorum
Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000)
cityPlaces.note: Site unknown within Trastevere.

cityPlaces.name: Office of the Urban Prefect in the Templum Pacis
cityPlaces.summary: The hall on the south-east side of Vespasian's Templum Pacis, whose wall carried the Severan Marble Plan (203-211), is widely taken to have housed the records of the urban prefecture and the city survey. The plan's 150 marble slabs, 18 by 13 m, show every building at 1:240.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed. 2010)
Tucci, The Temple of Peace in Rome (2017)
Stanford Digital Forma Urbis Romae Project
cityPlaces.note: The hall survives as the rear wall of Santi Cosma e Damiano (527). Function as prefecture office is inferred.

cityPlaces.name: Tribunal of the Urban Prefect 'in Tellure'
cityPlaces.summary: In late antiquity the urban prefect heard cases at the secretarium by the Temple of Tellus on the Carinae; the acts of the martyrs and the Theodosian Code place trials 'in Tellure'. The temple had been built in 268 BC on the site of Spurius Cassius' razed house.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Tellus, Aedes
Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000) s.v. Secretarium Tellurense
Krautheimer, Rome: Profile of a City, 312-1308 (1980)
cityPlaces.note: Near San Pietro in Vincoli and Via del Colosseo.

cityPlaces.name: Statio Annonae
cityPlaces.summary: Late 4th-century arcaded hall of the grain office by the Forum Boarium, whose columns are still embedded in the walls of Santa Maria in Cosmedin. It administered the annona, the free and subsidised food supply of the city; by the late 6th century it had become a diaconia distributing church relief.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Statio Annonae
Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed. 2010)
Krautheimer, Rome: Profile of a City, 312-1308 (1980)
cityPlaces.note: Earlier offices of the praefectus annonae stood nearby around the Ara Maxima.

cityPlaces.name: Statio Aquarum at the Lacus Iuturnae
cityPlaces.summary: Office of the curator aquarum, moved in the early 4th century to rooms beside the spring of Juturna in the Forum. Inscriptions of the curators of 328 and later were found in the rooms; the water board controlled the aqueducts until their cutting by the Goths in 537.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Statio Aquarum
Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed. 2010)
Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000)

cityPlaces.name: Mensa Ponderaria (official weights 'ad Castoris')
cityPlaces.summary: The Temple of Castor in the Forum served as the bureau of weights and measures: official bronze and stone weights are inscribed as checked 'ad Castoris', and the podium chambers held deposits and bankers' strongboxes. Here traders had scales and measures tested against the public standards.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Castor, Aedes
Platner and Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929)
Nielsen and Poulsen, The Temple of Castor and Pollux I (1992)
cityPlaces.note: Mensa ponderaria is the generic term for a standard-measure table; the Roman one sat at this temple.

cityPlaces.name: Lautumiae (state prison)
cityPlaces.summary: Old quarry-prison on the north-west side of the Forum, below the Arx, next to the Carcer. Livy names it in the fire of 210 BC with the Forum Piscarium, and Carthaginian hostages were kept here; the area was cleared for the Forum of Caesar.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Lautumiae
Platner and Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929)

cityPlaces.name: Curia Hostilia (Senate house)
cityPlaces.summary: The traditional Senate house at the north side of the Comitium, facing south. The Senate met here through the Republic; it was burned by Clodius' supporters who cremated his body inside in January 52 BC, rebuilt by Faustus Sulla and cleared by Caesar for the Curia Iulia.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Bonnefond-Coudry, Le Sénat de la République romaine (1989)

cityPlaces.name: Curia Iulia (Senate house)
cityPlaces.summary: Caesar's new Senate house, dedicated by Augustus in 29 BC and rebuilt by Diocletian after the fire of 283. The last recorded act of the Senate is the reception of Phocas' images in 603; Honorius I turned the hall into the church of Sant'Adriano in 630.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Bonnefond-Coudry, Le Sénat de la République romaine (1989)

cityPlaces.name: Curia of Pompey
cityPlaces.summary: Hall at the east end of Pompey's portico, used by the Senate while the Curia Hostilia lay in ruins. Caesar was murdered here at the foot of Pompey's statue on 15 March 44 BC; Augustus walled it up as an accursed place.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Bonnefond-Coudry, Le Sénat de la République romaine (1989)

cityPlaces.name: Temple of Concord (Senate meetings)
cityPlaces.summary: A frequent meeting place of the Senate: Cicero's fourth Catilinarian (63 BC) and the condemnation of Sejanus (AD 31) were delivered here.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Bonnefond-Coudry, Le Sénat de la République romaine (1989)

cityPlaces.name: Capitoline Temple (first Senate meeting of the year)
cityPlaces.summary: The new consuls convened the Senate in the Temple of Jupiter Optimus Maximus on the first day of their year, after their sacrifice.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Bonnefond-Coudry, Le Sénat de la République romaine (1989)

cityPlaces.name: Temple of Bellona (Senate outside the pomerium)
cityPlaces.summary: Because it stood outside the pomerium, the Senate met here to receive generals still holding imperium and foreign embassies not admitted to the city. Sulla had 6,000 prisoners massacred in the Villa Publica within earshot of a meeting here in 82 BC.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Bonnefond-Coudry, Le Sénat de la République romaine (1989)

cityPlaces.name: Temple of Apollo Medicus (Senate outside the pomerium)
cityPlaces.summary: Next to the Temple of Bellona in the Prata Flaminia, also used for Senate meetings outside the pomerium, especially to debate triumphs.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Bonnefond-Coudry, Le Sénat de la République romaine (1989)

cityPlaces.name: Temple of Jupiter Stator (Senate meetings)
cityPlaces.summary: Here, on 8 November 63 BC, Cicero delivered the First Catilinarian to a Senate guarded by armed men, with Catiline present.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Bonnefond-Coudry, Le Sénat de la République romaine (1989)

cityPlaces.name: Temple of Fides (Senate meetings)
cityPlaces.summary: On the Capitol near the Temple of Jupiter. The Senate was meeting here in 133 BC when Scipio Nasica led the senators out to kill Tiberius Gracchus.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Bonnefond-Coudry, Le Sénat de la République romaine (1989)

cityPlaces.name: Temple of Tellus (Senate of 17 March 44 BC)
cityPlaces.summary: On the Carinae near Antony's house. Two days after Caesar's murder the Senate met here and, on Cicero's motion, voted an amnesty for the assassins while confirming Caesar's acts.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Bonnefond-Coudry, Le Sénat de la République romaine (1989)

cityPlaces.name: Temple of Castor (Senate meetings)
cityPlaces.summary: The Senate occasionally met in the temple, whose high podium also served as a speakers' platform for assemblies in the Forum.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Bonnefond-Coudry, Le Sénat de la République romaine (1989)

cityPlaces.name: Library of the Temple of Apollo (Augustus' Senate)
cityPlaces.summary: In his old age Augustus often held Senate meetings in the Latin library hall of the Palatine Temple of Apollo, and revised the senatorial lists there.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Bonnefond-Coudry, Le Sénat de la République romaine (1989)

cityPlaces.name: Temple of Mars Ultor (Senate on war and triumphs)
cityPlaces.summary: Augustus decreed that the Senate should deliberate here on wars and triumphs, and that victorious generals should dedicate their sceptres and crowns to Mars.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Bonnefond-Coudry, Le Sénat de la République romaine (1989)

cityPlaces.name: Senaculum
cityPlaces.summary: Open waiting place of the senators between the Comitium and the Temple of Concord, where they assembled before meetings in the Curia.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Bonnefond-Coudry, Le Sénat de la République romaine (1989)

cityPlaces.name: Secretarium Senatus
cityPlaces.summary: Late-antique court room behind the Curia, where the Senate tried senators. It was restored by the urban prefect Epiphanius in 412 after the Gothic sack; the church of Santa Martina later occupied it.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Bonnefond-Coudry, Le Sénat de la République romaine (1989)

cityPlaces.name: Macellum (republican meat and provisions market)
cityPlaces.summary: The general provisions market behind the Basilica Aemilia, built by the censor M. Fulvius Nobilior in 179 BC by surrounding the older fish and delicacy markets with shops. Varro describes it as the union of the specialised fora. It burned in 64 and Vespasian's Templum Pacis was built over its site.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Macellum
Platner and Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929)
De Ruyt, Macellum (1983)
cityPlaces.note: Position under the north-west part of the Templum Pacis, reached from the Argiletum.

cityPlaces.name: Forum Piscarium (fish market)
cityPlaces.summary: The fish market north of the Forum, where Plautus' characters bargain for fish. It burned with the Lautumiae and the Atrium Regium in the arson of 210 BC and was rebuilt, then absorbed in 179 BC into Fulvius' Macellum.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Forum Piscarium
Platner and Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929)

cityPlaces.name: Forum Cuppedinis (delicacies market)
cityPlaces.summary: Market for luxury foods and dainties (cuppedia) near the Sacra Via, north-east of the Forum. Varro derives its name from the dainties or from a knight Cuppes whose house stood there; it became part of the Macellum complex.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Forum Cuppedinis
Platner and Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929)

cityPlaces.name: Macellum Liviae
cityPlaces.summary: Provisions market on the Esquiline just outside the Porta Esquilina, dedicated by Tiberius in 7 BC in Livia's name. It served the new Esquiline quarter; Valentinian, Valens and Gratian restored it in 364-367.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Macellum Liviae
Platner and Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929)
Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000)
De Ruyt, Macellum (1983)
cityPlaces.note: Placed between the Arch of Gallienus and Santa Maria Maggiore's eastern slope, near San Vito; site not excavated.

cityPlaces.name: Macellum Magnum
cityPlaces.summary: Great market on the Caelian dedicated by Nero in 59 and shown on his coins as a two-storey building with a domed central pavilion. Santo Stefano Rotondo (c. 470) is commonly thought to stand on its site and perhaps to echo its round plan.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Macellum Magnum
Platner and Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929)
De Ruyt, Macellum (1983)
cityPlaces.note: Identification with the site of Santo Stefano Rotondo is debated.

cityPlaces.name: Forum Esquilinum
cityPlaces.summary: Market square just inside the Porta Esquilina. In 88 BC Sulla's troops entering the city fought Marius' supporters here; it later appears among the sights of Region V.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Forum Esquilinum
Platner and Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929)

cityPlaces.name: Forum Suarium (pork market)
cityPlaces.summary: Pork market in the Campus Agrippae, Region VII, under a tribunus fori suarii and the guild of the suarii. Aurelian added free pork to the dole in the 270s and the distribution was run from here; Valentinian III still regulated it in 452.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Forum Suarium
Barnish, 'Pigs, plebeians and potentes', PBSR 55 (1987)
cityPlaces.note: Site not found; placed by the Castra Urbana whose soldiers supervised it.

cityPlaces.name: Forum Vinarium (wine market)
cityPlaces.summary: Wholesale wine market known from inscriptions of merchants 'a foro vinario'. It lay near the river where wine arrived by barge, probably by the Emporium below the Aventine or across the river at Ripa.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Forum Vinarium
Platner and Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929)
cityPlaces.note: Location unknown; placed at the north end of the Emporium quays.

cityPlaces.name: Ciconiae Nixae (wine landing and tax office)
cityPlaces.summary: Landing place in the north-west Campus Martius, named after a monument of 'leaning storks', where wine shipments were taxed. Aurelian's subsidised wine was stored in the porticoes of the Temple of Sol and distributed through this office.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Ciconiae Nixae
Coarelli, Rome and Environs: An Archaeological Guide (2007)
cityPlaces.note: Coarelli places it near San Salvatore in Lauro.

cityPlaces.name: Forum Pistorum (bakers' market)
cityPlaces.summary: Bakers' market listed in Region XIII (Aventinus), presumably near the mills and grain warehouses of the Emporium.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Forum Pistorum
Platner and Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929)
cityPlaces.note: Location within Region XIII unknown.

cityPlaces.name: Forum Boarium (cattle market)
cityPlaces.summary: The cattle market by the river harbour, the oldest trading place of the city, where the Etruscan and Greek traders met the Latins at the ford below the Tiber Island. It stayed a market square through antiquity.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Forum Boarium
Coarelli, Rome and Environs: An Archaeological Guide (2007)

cityPlaces.name: Forum Holitorium (vegetable market)
cityPlaces.summary: Vegetable and herb market outside the Porta Carmentalis, between the Capitol and the river, with the temples of Janus, Spes and Juno Sospita along its west side.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Forum Holitorium
Coarelli, Rome and Environs: An Archaeological Guide (2007)

cityPlaces.name: Porticus Minucia Frumentaria (grain dole)
cityPlaces.summary: The distribution centre of the frumentationes, the free monthly grain ration (5 modii) for some 200,000 registered citizens. Recipients carried tesserae naming a day and one of 45 numbered doors (ostia) of the portico. Aurelian replaced grain with daily bread handed out from steps (gradus) across the city.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Porticus Minucia
Coarelli, Rome and Environs: An Archaeological Guide (2007)
Virlouvet, Tessera frumentaria (1995)
cityPlaces.note: Coarelli identifies the Frumentaria with the large portico east of Largo Argentina along Via delle Botteghe Oscure; Manacorda prefers the Crypta Balbi area. Distribution there probably began under Claudius.

cityPlaces.name: Bakery of Marcus Vergilius Eurysaces
cityPlaces.summary: The freedman baker and contractor for public bread built his tomb (c. 30 BC) at the fork of the Via Praenestina and Labicana, its frieze showing grain weighed, milled by donkeys, kneaded, baked and delivered to officials. His bakery probably stood nearby at the city edge.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Sepulcrum Eurysacis
Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed. 2010)
Petersen, The Freedman in Roman Art and Art History (2006)
cityPlaces.note: Bakery site inferred from the tomb; the tomb itself is in buildings (tomb_of_eurysaces). Regionary Catalogues count 254 bakeries (pistrina) in the city.

cityPlaces.name: Mills of the Janiculum
cityPlaces.summary: Water-mills driven by the Aqua Traiana on the Janiculum slope, partly excavated under the American Academy and along Via Garibaldi. In 537 the Goths cut the aqueducts and Belisarius kept the city fed by mounting mills on boats moored in the Tiber.
scholarship: Wilson, 'Water-mills on the Janiculum', MAAR 45 (2000)
Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed. 2010)

cityPlaces.name: Floating mills of Belisarius
cityPlaces.summary: When the Goths cut the aqueducts in 537, Belisarius moored boats below the bridge at the Janiculum and hung mill-wheels between them in the current; the Goths sent logs and corpses downstream to break them, and he answered with chains across the river.
scholarship: Wilson, 'Water-mills on the Janiculum', MAAR 45 (2000)
Krautheimer, Rome: Profile of a City, 312-1308 (1980)
cityPlaces.note: Near the Pons Aurelius (Ponte Sisto). Ship-mills remained typical of medieval Rome.

cityPlaces.name: Water-mill in the Baths of Caracalla
cityPlaces.summary: A water-mill driven by the outflow of the baths was installed in the underground service galleries of the Baths of Caracalla, one of the few urban mills known in Rome.
scholarship: Schiøler and Wikander, 'A Roman water-mill in the Baths of Caracalla', Opuscula Romana 14 (1983)
Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed. 2010)
cityPlaces.note: Date of installation uncertain (3rd-4th century).

cityPlaces.name: Horrea Agrippiana
cityPlaces.summary: Warehouse of three storeys around a courtyard at the foot of the Palatine on the Vicus Tuscus, built by Agrippa and rebuilt under Domitian. A shrine in the court held a statue base to the Genius horreorum Agrippianorum. Excavated in 1902-1904 by Boni beside San Teodoro.
scholarship: Rickman, Roman Granaries and Store Buildings (1971)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Horrea Agrippiana
Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed. 2010)
Astolfi, Guidobaldi and Pronti, 'Horrea Agrippiana', ArchCl 30 (1978)

cityPlaces.name: Horrea Germaniciana
cityPlaces.summary: Listed with the Horrea Agrippiana in Region VIII; presumably named after Germanicus and standing beside them along the Vicus Tuscus towards the Velabrum.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Horrea Germaniciana
Rickman, Roman Granaries and Store Buildings (1971)
cityPlaces.note: Placed adjacent to the Agrippiana.

cityPlaces.name: Horrea Piperataria (pepper warehouses)
cityPlaces.summary: Spice warehouses built by Domitian on the Sacra Via for pepper and eastern spices. Their burning in the fire of 192 destroyed the stock of many merchants and the books Galen kept there. Maxentius levelled them for his Basilica Nova; their rooms lie under it.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Horrea Piperataria
Rickman, Roman Granaries and Store Buildings (1971)
Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed. 2010)

cityPlaces.name: Horrea Vespasiani
cityPlaces.summary: Warehouses attributed to Vespasian in the Chronographer of 354, probably near the Sacra Via close to the Horrea Piperataria, serving the luxury trade of the Velia.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Horrea Vespasiani
Rickman, Roman Granaries and Store Buildings (1971)

cityPlaces.name: Horrea Galbana (Sulpicia)
cityPlaces.summary: The largest warehouse complex of Rome, about 167 by 146 m around three long courtyards behind the Emporium, with some 140 rooms per floor for grain, oil and wine. Built around 100 BC on land of the Sulpicii Galbae, perhaps by Ser. Sulpicius Galba (cos. 108 BC), and enlarged under the emperor Galba. Shown on the Marble Plan.
scholarship: Rickman, Roman Granaries and Store Buildings (1971)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Horrea Galbana
Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed. 2010)
Stanford Digital Forma Urbis Romae Project

cityPlaces.name: Horrea Lolliana
cityPlaces.summary: Warehouse with two courtyards on the Tiber quay of the Emporium, named on fragment 25 of the Marble Plan, between the Porticus Aemilia and the river.
scholarship: Rickman, Roman Granaries and Store Buildings (1971)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Horrea Lolliana
Stanford Digital Forma Urbis Romae Project
cityPlaces.note: Builder perhaps a Lollius of the Augustan period.

cityPlaces.name: Horrea Seiana
cityPlaces.summary: Warehouse known from inscriptions to the Genius of the horrea Seiana found near Testaccio; it probably stood south of the Horrea Galbana, perhaps named after Seius Strabo, father of Sejanus.
scholarship: Rickman, Roman Granaries and Store Buildings (1971)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Horrea Seiana

cityPlaces.name: Horrea Aniciana
cityPlaces.summary: Warehouse named after the Anicii (or Anicetus), known from inscriptions found in the Testaccio district.
scholarship: Rickman, Roman Granaries and Store Buildings (1971)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)

cityPlaces.name: Horrea Candelaria
cityPlaces.summary: Store for candles and tallow, shown on fragment 44 of the Marble Plan as a building around a large open area. Its location in the city has not been fixed.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Horrea Candelaria
Stanford Digital Forma Urbis Romae Project (fragment 44)
cityPlaces.note: Placed provisionally in the Velabrum; the true position is unknown.

cityPlaces.name: Horrea Chartaria (paper warehouses)
cityPlaces.summary: Warehouse for papyrus and writing material listed in Region IV (Templum Pacis), conveniently near the booksellers of the Argiletum and the Vicus Sandaliarius.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Horrea Chartaria
Rickman, Roman Granaries and Store Buildings (1971)
cityPlaces.note: Exact site unknown within Region IV.

cityPlaces.name: Horrea of Q. Tineius Sacerdos
cityPlaces.summary: Private warehouse of the senator Q. Tineius Sacerdos (cos. 158 or his homonymous son, cos. 192), known from an inscription; likely in the Emporium district.
scholarship: Rickman, Roman Granaries and Store Buildings (1971)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)

cityPlaces.name: Horrea Ummidiana
cityPlaces.summary: Warehouse named after the Ummidii, a senatorial family, known from inscriptions and the Marble Plan tradition; probably on the Aventine side of the city.
scholarship: Rickman, Roman Granaries and Store Buildings (1971)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
cityPlaces.note: Location unknown; placed on the lower Aventine towards the Porta Raudusculana.

cityPlaces.name: Horrea Sempronia (Gracchan granaries)
cityPlaces.summary: Public granaries built under Gaius Gracchus' grain law of 123 BC to store the grain sold at a fixed low price to citizens. Their site is unknown; most scholars look to the river below the Aventine.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Horrea Sempronia
Rickman, Roman Granaries and Store Buildings (1971)

cityPlaces.name: Horrea Volusiana
cityPlaces.summary: Warehouse of the Volusii Saturnini, a great senatorial family of the early empire with a household of many hundreds of slaves, known from inscriptions; probably on the right bank near the Via Portuensis landing.
scholarship: Rickman, Roman Granaries and Store Buildings (1971)

cityPlaces.name: Warehouse under Santa Maria in Via Lata
cityPlaces.summary: A large arcaded building of the late empire on the Via Lata, interpreted as a public warehouse or porticus; its ground floor later housed the diaconia of Santa Maria in Via Lata.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Krautheimer, Rome: Profile of a City, 312-1308 (1980)
Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed. 2010)
cityPlaces.note: Possibly part of the Saepta or the Porticus of the Via Lata complex.

cityPlaces.name: Latrine of Via Garibaldi
cityPlaces.summary: Public latrine on the Janiculum found in 1963 under the terrace in front of San Pietro in Montorio. A channel 0.4 m wide ran round three sides; the seats were probably wooden boards on supports. Frescoes and a geometric mosaic date it to the late 2nd or early 3rd century.
scholarship: Turismo Roma, Latrina romana di via Garibaldi
Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed. 2010)
cityPlaces.note: Turismo Roma gives 41.8934 N, which falls on lower Via Garibaldi; placed here by the church terrace described in the excavation reports.

cityPlaces.name: Latrine of the Forum of Caesar
cityPlaces.summary: Public latrine installed in the Trajanic rebuilding of the Forum of Caesar, in a room at its western corner by the Basilica Argentaria and the Clivus Argentarius, with marble seats along the walls over a flushing channel.
scholarship: Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed. 2010)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)

cityPlaces.name: Latrine at Largo Argentina
cityPlaces.summary: Public latrine of the imperial period behind Temples A and B at Largo Argentina, beside the remains of the Curia of Pompey, serving the crowds of the Porticus Minucia and the theatres.
scholarship: Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed. 2010)
Coarelli, Rome and Environs: An Archaeological Guide (2007)
cityPlaces.note: The Regionary Catalogues count 144 public latrines (foricae) in the city.

cityPlaces.name: Lacus Orphei
cityPlaces.summary: Public fountain on the Esquiline at the top of the Clivus Suburanus, decorated with a figure of Orpheus surrounded by enchanted beasts and birds. Martial tells his book to climb past it to reach Pliny the Younger's house.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Lacus Orphei
Platner and Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929)
cityPlaces.note: Near Santa Lucia in Selci and San Martino ai Monti.

cityPlaces.name: Lacus Promethei
cityPlaces.summary: Fountain with a statue group of Prometheus, listed in Region I (Porta Capena), probably on the Via Appia between the Porta Capena and the Baths of Caracalla.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Lacus Promethei
Platner and Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929)
cityPlaces.note: Site unknown within Region I.

cityPlaces.name: Lacus Pastoris
cityPlaces.summary: Fountain 'of the Shepherd' listed in Region III (Isis et Serapis), in the valley east of the Colosseum near the gladiatorial schools.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Lacus Pastoris
Platner and Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929)
cityPlaces.note: Site unknown within Region III.

cityPlaces.name: Lacus Fundani
cityPlaces.summary: Fountain on the lower Quirinal, possibly named after a Fundanius; it gave its name to the area where, in 63 BC, Catilinarian conspirators were said to have met.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Lacus Fundani
Platner and Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929)
cityPlaces.note: Tacitus places Flavian fighting near it in AD 69.

cityPlaces.name: Lacus Servilius
cityPlaces.summary: Fountain basin at the west corner of the Basilica Iulia where the Vicus Iugarius entered the Forum. Sulla displayed the heads of the proscribed senators here in 82 BC; Agrippa adorned it with a hydra statue.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Lacus Servilius
Platner and Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929)

cityPlaces.name: Lacus Ganymedis
cityPlaces.summary: Fountain with a statue of Ganymede listed in the Regionary Catalogues, probably in the Campus Agrippae along the Via Lata.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Lacus Ganymedis
cityPlaces.note: Region and site uncertain.

cityPlaces.name: Fons Camenarum (Spring of the Camenae)
cityPlaces.summary: Sacred spring in the grove of the Camenae and Egeria outside the Porta Capena, from which the Vestals drew the water for their rites. By Juvenal's day the grove was let to poor Jewish families.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Camenae
Platner and Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929)
cityPlaces.note: In the valley between the Caelian and the Aventine, by the Via Appia.

cityPlaces.name: Fons Mercurii
cityPlaces.summary: Spring near the Porta Capena where merchants on the Ides of May sprinkled their goods and heads with laurel dipped in its water, asking Mercury to forgive their lies.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Fons Mercurii

cityPlaces.name: Agrippa's fountains of 33 BC (Campus Martius example)
cityPlaces.summary: As aedile in 33 BC Agrippa built 700 basins (lacus), 105 fountains and 130 distribution towers, many decorated with columns and statues. This marker stands for the network in the Campus Martius fed by his Aqua Virgo (19 BC).
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Evans, Water Distribution in Ancient Rome (1994)
cityPlaces.note: Symbolic marker; the 4th-century Regionary Catalogues count 1,352 lacus in the city.

cityPlaces.name: Compitum Acilium
cityPlaces.summary: Crossroads shrine on the Velia. In 219 BC the state bought a shop here for Archagathus, the first Greek doctor in Rome. Its Augustan marble aedicula, dedicated by the vicomagistri in 5 BC, was found in 1932 when Via dell'Impero cut through the Velia.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Compitum Acilium
Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000)
Lott, The Neighborhoods of Augustan Rome (2004)
cityPlaces.note: Destroyed in the fire of 64 or the Neronian rebuilding; remains removed.

cityPlaces.name: Altar of the Lares of the Vicus Sandaliarius
cityPlaces.summary: Marble compital altar of 2 BC (now in the Uffizi) from the Vicus Sandaliarius, the street of sandal-makers and booksellers in Region IV. Its reliefs show Augustus taking the augural staff with Gaius Caesar and Livia, the official image of the new Lares Augusti cult.
scholarship: Lott, The Neighborhoods of Augustan Rome (2004)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Vicus Sandaliarius
cityPlaces.note: Provenance within the street not recorded; placed near the Temple of Tellus.

cityPlaces.name: Altar of the Lares of the Vicus Aesculeti
cityPlaces.summary: Compital altar dedicated in AD 2 by four magistri of the Vicus Aesculeti, found in situ in 1888 at the crossroads under Via Arenula in the southern Campus Martius. Its relief shows the vicomagistri sacrificing a pig and a bull.
scholarship: Lott, The Neighborhoods of Augustan Rome (2004)
Haselberger et al., Mapping Augustan Rome (2002)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Vicus Aesculeti
cityPlaces.note: Now in the Capitoline collections (Centrale Montemartini).

cityPlaces.name: Sacellum Larum (shrine of the Lares Praestites)
cityPlaces.summary: Shrine of the guardian Lares of the city at the top of the Sacra Via, at the north-east corner of the Palatine. It marked a corner of the Palatine pomerium of Romulus.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Lares, Sacellum
Platner and Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929)

cityPlaces.name: Signum Vortumni (shrine of Vertumnus)
cityPlaces.summary: Bronze statue of the Etruscan god Vertumnus in a small shrine where the Vicus Tuscus left the Forum behind the Temple of Castor. Propertius gives the statue a speaking voice; booksellers like the Sosii had stalls beside it.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Vortumnus, Signum
Platner and Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929)
cityPlaces.note: A base re-inscribed under Diocletian was found near the spot.

cityPlaces.name: Tigillum Sororium
cityPlaces.summary: Wooden beam across a lane on the slope of the Carinae, under which the surviving Horatius was said to have passed to purify himself after killing his sister. The beam was renewed at public expense through antiquity.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Tigillum Sororium
Platner and Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929)

cityPlaces.name: Ara Aii Locutii
cityPlaces.summary: Altar to the 'Speaking Voice' at the foot of the Palatine near the Temple of Vesta, built where a plebeian heard a voice in the night warning of the coming Gauls in 391 BC, a warning the magistrates ignored.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Aius Locutius
Platner and Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929)

cityPlaces.name: Puteal Libonis (Puteal Scribonianum)
cityPlaces.summary: A fenced well-head in the Forum near the Arch of Fabius, struck by lightning and enclosed by a Scribonius Libo. Moneylenders, debtors and the praetor's tribunal gathered here, so Horace uses it as shorthand for the world of business.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Puteal Libonis
Platner and Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929)

cityPlaces.name: Ianus Medius (bankers' exchange)
cityPlaces.summary: The middle of the arched passages beside the Basilica Aemilia, the meeting point of bankers and financiers. Horace and Cicero use 'the Ianus medius' as Romans now use 'Wall Street'.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Ianus Medius
Platner and Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929)

cityPlaces.name: Library of Asinius Pollio (Atrium Libertatis)
cityPlaces.summary: The first public library of Rome, founded by Asinius Pollio from the spoils of his Illyrian campaign in the restored Atrium Libertatis, with Greek and Latin sections and portraits of authors, including the living Varro.
scholarship: Houston, Inside Roman Libraries (2014)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Atrium Libertatis
Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000)
cityPlaces.note: The Atrium Libertatis is placed on the saddle between Capitol and Quirinal later cut for Trajan's Forum, where its functions passed to the Basilica Ulpia.

cityPlaces.name: Libraries of the Porticus Octaviae
cityPlaces.summary: Greek and Latin libraries founded by Octavia in memory of her son Marcellus (d. 23 BC) inside her portico, managed by the grammarian C. Melissus. They burned in the fire of 80 and were restored.
scholarship: Houston, Inside Roman Libraries (2014)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Porticus Octaviae

cityPlaces.name: Palatine Library of Apollo
cityPlaces.summary: Twin halls for Greek and Latin books beside Augustus' Temple of Apollo, with niches for book cupboards and portrait medallions of authors. Ovid's exiled books were barred from it. The temple burned in 363 and the library with it.
scholarship: Houston, Inside Roman Libraries (2014)
Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed. 2010)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Bibliotheca Apollinis Palatini

cityPlaces.name: Library of the Temple of Divus Augustus
cityPlaces.summary: Library attached to the temple of the deified Augustus behind the Basilica Iulia, with a colossal bronze Apollo 50 feet high.
scholarship: Houston, Inside Roman Libraries (2014)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Augustus, Divus, Templum
cityPlaces.note: The temple's site is unlocated; placed below the Palatine's north-west corner.

cityPlaces.name: Library of the Domus Tiberiana
cityPlaces.summary: Imperial library in the palace on the Palatine above the Forum where Gellius and his friends sat reading and arguing over Latin usage.
scholarship: Houston, Inside Roman Libraries (2014)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)

cityPlaces.name: Library of the Templum Pacis
cityPlaces.summary: Library in Vespasian's Temple of Peace, a meeting place of scholars and doctors. Galen lost books he had stored there and in the nearby warehouses in the fire of 192; Severus restored the complex.
scholarship: Houston, Inside Roman Libraries (2014)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Pax, Templum
Tucci, The Temple of Peace in Rome (2017)

cityPlaces.name: Bibliotheca Ulpia
cityPlaces.summary: The two library halls flanking Trajan's Column, one Greek and one Latin, with niches for book cupboards, which also held state archives such as praetors' edicts. Sidonius in the 450s and Venantius Fortunatus a century later still speak of readings and statues there.
scholarship: Houston, Inside Roman Libraries (2014)
Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed. 2010)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Bibliotheca Ulpia

cityPlaces.name: Library at the Pantheon (Julius Africanus)
cityPlaces.summary: Julius Africanus, the Christian chronographer, designed 'the beautiful library in the Pantheon' for Severus Alexander, according to a papyrus fragment of his Kestoi. It was probably in the Baths of Agrippa or the Baths of Alexander next door.
scholarship: Houston, Inside Roman Libraries (2014)
cityPlaces.note: Exact position near the Pantheon uncertain.

cityPlaces.name: Libraries of the Baths of Caracalla
cityPlaces.summary: Two halls in the enclosure of the Baths of Caracalla, on either side of the stadium-shaped garden, with wall niches for book cupboards; baths combined bathing, exercise, lecture rooms and reading.
scholarship: Houston, Inside Roman Libraries (2014)
Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed. 2010)
DeLaine, The Baths of Caracalla (1997)

cityPlaces.name: Library of the Baths of Trajan
cityPlaces.summary: Exedra on the south-west side of the enclosure of the Baths of Trajan fitted with tiered niches for books, among the clearest library rooms in Rome.
scholarship: Houston, Inside Roman Libraries (2014)
Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed. 2010)

cityPlaces.name: Library of the Baths of Diocletian
cityPlaces.summary: The Historia Augusta claims that the books of the Bibliotheca Ulpia were in its day kept in the Baths of Diocletian, suggesting a library hall there.
scholarship: Houston, Inside Roman Libraries (2014)
cityPlaces.note: Room not identified.

cityPlaces.name: Library on the Capitol
cityPlaces.summary: Late sources record a library on the Capitol destroyed by lightning and fire under Commodus.
scholarship: Houston, Inside Roman Libraries (2014)

cityPlaces.name: Library of Lucullus
cityPlaces.summary: Lucullus opened his library of books captured in the Mithridatic War to Greek scholars in his gardens on the Pincian, with walks and study rooms; Cicero and Cato read there.
scholarship: Houston, Inside Roman Libraries (2014)
cityPlaces.note: In the Horti Lucullani; the gardens themselves are in buildings.

cityPlaces.name: Library of Pope Agapetus
cityPlaces.summary: Pope Agapetus and Cassiodorus planned a Christian school at Rome around 535; Agapetus built a library on the Clivus Scauri, recorded in a verse inscription. A hall beside the monastery of Sant'Andrea has been identified with it.
scholarship: Krautheimer, Rome: Profile of a City, 312-1308 (1980)
Marrou, 'Autour de la bibliothèque du pape Agapit', MEFR 48 (1931)

cityPlaces.name: Archive of Pope Damasus (San Lorenzo in Damaso)
cityPlaces.summary: Pope Damasus built a church and new buildings for the archives (archivis nova tecta) of the Roman church by the Theatre of Pompey, as his own verse inscription states; the site is now covered by the Palazzo della Cancelleria.
scholarship: Krautheimer, Rome: Profile of a City, 312-1308 (1980)
Pietri, Roma Christiana (1976)

cityPlaces.name: Lateran Scrinium (papal archive and library)
cityPlaces.summary: Archive and library of the bishop of Rome in the Lateran episcopium. Gregory the Great's registers of letters were kept here, and 7th-century popes sent books from it to England and Gaul.
scholarship: Krautheimer, Rome: Profile of a City, 312-1308 (1980)

cityPlaces.name: Athenaeum of Hadrian
cityPlaces.summary: Hadrian's institute for rhetoric, poetry and philosophy, where orators and poets declaimed. Three large halls with tiered marble seating for about 900 people were found in 2008-2012 under Piazza Venezia during work on Metro C.
scholarship: Egidi, Serlorenzi and others, excavation reports for Metro C at Piazza Venezia (2012)
cityPlaces.note: Identification with the Athenaeum is the excavators' and widely accepted.

cityPlaces.name: School of Plotinus (house of Gemina)
cityPlaces.summary: From 244 until his last illness Plotinus taught Neoplatonism in Rome in the house of the widow Gemina, where senators like Rogatianus, the physician Eustochius and Porphyry heard him; the emperor Gallienus favoured him.
scholarship: Armstrong, Plotinus (Loeb) introduction
cityPlaces.note: The site of Gemina's house is unknown; placed on the Esquiline by convention only.

cityPlaces.name: Schola Xanthi
cityPlaces.summary: Meeting hall of the scribes and heralds of the curule aediles at the foot of the Clivus Capitolinus beside the Temple of Saturn, restored by the freedman Bebryx Drusianus and Aulus Fabius Xanthus.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Schola Xanthi
Platner and Ashby, A Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1929)

cityPlaces.name: Schools in the Forum shops
cityPlaces.summary: Elementary schools (ludi litterarum) were held in the shops round the Forum. Livy places the girl Verginia walking to school here in 449 BC when the decemvir Appius Claudius had her seized.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)

cityPlaces.name: School of Verrius Flaccus
cityPlaces.summary: Augustus appointed the grammarian Verrius Flaccus to teach his grandsons, and moved his whole school into the atrium of the house of Catulus on the Palatine, on condition that he took no new pupils.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
